utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon ladies and gentlemen. Before we have the witness, are there any matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention to this Bench? Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted the record to reflect and the Trial Chamber to be informed that counsel for Blagojevic and counsel for Mr. Jokic have met with the Prosecutor today, and we have come to an agreement about disclosure of the intercepts. And the ability of our expert witness to examine the raw material and Mr. McCloskey met with us and Mr. Waespi. We came to an agreement that at a future date they would provide their archived original raw data to the laboratory here in Holland that the OTP has used. We've agreed to use the same laboratory that they've used and we'll have our expert come and be present with the OTP raw material at the Dutch lab at a future time. So the complete analysis of the intercept tapes would probably not take place until probably the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything that the Prosecution would like to raise on this same issue? Ms. Issa?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour. Not at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Well, could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand that you have been in The Hague for quite a long time. We will try our best to send you back home tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll take the hint from the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Ms. Sinatra: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra, you may start.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dobar dan.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go back to some questioning regarding the UHER reel-to-reel tape recorder and I just want to ask you some technical points about the recorder itself, if you don't mind us going back.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't mind. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The UHER tape recorder that you used, did it use -- it used quarter inch Mylar tape or was it acetate tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please believe me, Ms. Sinatra, I don't really know much about this. All I know is that it could be played for a few hours and I think it was 16 millimetres wide, like a videotape. Of course I know what it looks like because I worked with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was a brown colour exposed tape, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, the tape was such that you had a feed line on it that you put into the receiving reel and you had to bend it like this before you could start activating the reel-to-reel action?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Madam. And we had to make a few turns for the tape to become taut.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you said -- I forgot how many centimetres you said the cassette was or the reel-to-reel tape was, but that's one of the smaller versions. I don't know if you know the rate between centimetres and inches, but would it be equivalent to a five-inch tape, reel-to-reel? No?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't go into the dimensions in inches. It was 16 millimetres, so you can calculate that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not really adept at that at the moment. Your reels were plastic or metal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember there were metal ones, but I think there were also plastic ones, so it would be both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was a portable machine that you used? It wasn't attached to the wall? It sat on the desk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the desk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you maintain this UHER equipment yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. The technical part, the repairs of the machines, what was inside the machines, no, I didn't deal with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a regular maintenance schedule for the machines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We regularly cleaned the heads after playing a few tapes. We would do that once a week or more often if necessary, and we would use cotton wool and alcohol to clean them. And when necessary, they would be sent to the command for servicing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the machine that you were using was a two-headed machine, too, wasn't it, which means one head was for erasing and the second head was for recording and playback?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And there was also a rubber wheel on which magnetic dust would collect and we had to clean that from time to time because it would get very dirty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that that was cleaned about once a week. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also stated that a lot of the reel-to-reel tapes that you were using had been donated to you from a radio station. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1995, the radio station had gone to cassettes or CDs to play for their radio station, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know whether they were just donated because they were extinct for the radio station or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the reason. But they seemed to have had a large amount of them that they didn't need.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know that they were probably stored somewhere at the radio station before they were donated to the military. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either, Madam. I don't know anything about the taking over of the tapes, but we could tell from their content that they came from the radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, you do know that a very microscopic amount of dirt can affect the quality of a recording. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this too: When you originally recorded the intercepted conversation on the UHER reel-to-reel and you marked that the conversation had to be listened to again, you took the tape off of the original machine and listened to it somewhere else, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, that's not how it was. The tape was listened to on the same machine on which the material had been recorded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I understand that now. Okay. I'm going to go back to the general precept of the war. You know that everybody and most of the intercepts that you intercepted from the VRS, most of them came from the hand-held Motorolas, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I wouldn't agree with you that all the intercepted conversations during the war came from hand-held Motorolas, because these were radio relay connections, so they were telephone connections, that is, referring to the period we are discussing now. At the beginning of the war, I had activities connected to the matters you have just mentioned, things that happened directly on the battle front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, just for clarification for the Trial Chamber, there's a big difference between an intercept from a communications centre like Okresanica versus the tactical intercepts on the front. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a tactical intercept involves someone crawling around on his stomach, doesn't it, dodging bullets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that during 1995, the BiH army had a severe personnel shortage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a certain problem. Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the BiH army didn't have any mobile interception units, did they, the trucks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understood your question this time. Could you please -- are you talking about the trucks we had or the trucks from which there were communications? Are you referring to trucks belonging to my unit?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I know your unit did not have a mobile interception unit or communications centre. I know your unit did not. But the BiH army didn't have any mobile communications centres, such as the JNA and the VRS had, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say if we're talking about the whole army, I'm not really interested in that, but my unit had a blue van.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the blue van was a mobile communications centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't a mobile communications centre. It was used to transport staff and appropriate equipment to a separate location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And you also had another problem in the BiH army in 1995, and believe me, I understand the conditions at the time, but you didn't have -- you had a shortage of spare parts from all the communications equipment, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go back to -- we discussed antennas yesterday, but I just want to clarify that the antenna that you had, it was a directional antenna, was it, or was it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the antenna you showed yesterday. That was a scanner antenna, but we didn't use that antenna at this location. The equipment refers to the beginning of the war, the equipment we had at the very outset. Later it all changed. To be quite specific, at the location I worked in in the period now under discussion, we used directional antennas of the Yagi type. And there was also an original military antenna, RRU-800.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the equipment that you described during your testimony in Krstic had to do with 1992; whereas, the equipment that we're talking about in 1995, you had already acquired a directional antenna. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, it says there what type of equipment we started out with. Don't let us get confused. The equipment we had in 1995 were Yagi antenna for RRU-1 and a Yagi antenna for RRU-800 and we also had a military antenna for RRU-800.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a military antenna is just a stationary antenna. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All these antennas were stationary. They were on masts which had nylon ropes. It was all done very properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did say that some of your antennas were homemade at one point, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean made by hand?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Made by amateur radio operators to fit the situation because you didn't have access to more sophisticated equipment at the time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, Madam, I'll have to explain a bit about this. We had original antennas from the television, which were completely adequate to the diameter, and it was RRU-800. The VHF range of the television covered VHF 3 and RRU-1, so it was quite adequate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The reason I want to talk to you about antennas again is that your maximum height of your antenna was 842 metres. Is that right? That's above sea level.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe even less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were in a mountainous region and Zvornik was in a valley region and had to go through a relay system. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know that radio waves only operate on line of sight links, unless you can beam up from a relay station. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't fully agree with that, because in the direct line up to optical visibility, there is a skein effect. There is a 20 per cent deviation, and that's what it says on the military equipment, which is why there is some confusion as to why we were able to get these signals. But we had very strong amplifiers in these antennas. These were called pre-amplifiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just based on your expertise and all your knowledge of radio waves, radio waves do not bend? They travel in a straight line, in a vector, don't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But I would like to add that these waves are also reflected from the first surface they come across.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you -- when you say -- I'm not going to go into reflective because that's beyond my knowledge at the moment, but I assume you mean like a relay station, beamed from one point to the next. Is that a reflection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not a reflection. That's a direct wave. You are now talking about direct waves. I would like to mention that radio relay equipment was of the duplex type. And therefore, they have a very strong component emitting and receiving signals. So there have to be strong filters called duplex filters to separate this, which is why the characteristics deteriorate. You get various types of signals, and that's why radio relay equipment cannot be as sensitive and have the same range as radio relay equipment in connection with a direct receiver whose receiving field is strengthened with additional equipment. And with the very sensitive Japanese equipment that we have listed and that we had at the time, which we used in our monitoring.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just going to try to sort out the information you just gave me. Are you saying that the base communications centres had much stronger receiving and transmitting abilities than a relay station used this duplex-type system? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't -- I don't want to go into the differences between radio relay stations and the equipment used in the communications centre. But if this is necessary, I'll do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask a basic question. We know that Zvornik had no direct communication with anybody. Everything that came from Zvornik had to go through a relay station 60 kilometres away. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the route, Madam. I don't know what the route was up to the relay station that you're talking about. They simply appeared to us as participants on this relay station. It would be very difficult at this moment to know the exact route for each participant. Very often even the people whose basic equipment this is have this problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's exactly what I wanted to say or wanted to ask you. Was from a relay station, you can't tell the location of the conversation or where it began, because it's going through another location. So you can't tell the difference between a communication from Vlasenica or one from Zvornik, can you, when they go through a relay station? You can't pinpoint the location of origination?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, my small unit was not given this task. These are elements for analysis carried out by others. Even had we wanted to, we would not have had time to deal with these matters. Our task was to receive information and to transmit it faithfully to those in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And through a relay station, you know that there's really no difference in the quality of the transmission, whether you pick it up from Zvornik or from Vlasenica. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the difference in the signal of one and the other participate, communicated by telephone whom you are listening to through a radio relay station is reflected precisely in who the transmitting component is, who is the participant from the relay station who is transmitting. The receiving party is the weaker party, if there is a difference. They can be of the same quality, but very often they weren't in practice. And another reason can be additional junctures between the participants up to the relay station where they were transported further on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think your answer was yes to my question, but I'm not quite sure, that you can't pinpoint the origination of an intercepted conversation from a relay station. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to bring out what is marked now -- I'd like to show you Defence exhibit -- I'm going to bring out 36.1/3 and 36.2/3. And, sir, I'm really sorry that I don't have a B/C/S translation of it right now, so I'm going to have to read the paragraph that I'm talking about to you, which is a short paragraph, Your Honour. And I would like, for the Court's attention and the Prosecution's attention, I'll be referring to a book that was referred to me by the Prosecution that has just been published here in -- I don't know how long it's been published. But it's a Dutch book by Cees Wiebes. The name of the book is: "Intelligence and the War in Bosnia, 1992 to 1995." And it's based upon the NIOD report that came out last year from the Dutch government. And I'm going to -- I think this must be 2 -- I mean 36.2. Page 299 of the book. I'm sorry -- yes, it is. I really apologise. I just got the book on Friday, so it was not possible to translate it between Friday and now. But page 99, the conclusion from the author of this book is that, "We know that an absolute minimum of ten channels had to be monitored continuously. That three persons were needed per channel for interception, transcription, and reporting, and that there was a rotation of three shifts a day and a ten-day working week. Then" -- I'm sorry, "a seven-day working week. Then at least 90 signal operators would have to be active at Okresanica, not to mention 15 to 20 staff for support, technology, security, catering, and so on. Hence, if there were 20 channels, probably a more realistic estimate, than at least 180 people would be needed. In reality, a maximum of 12 people worked at Okresanica. Most of the communications were re-recorded on tape. It seems, therefore, that a near realtime analysis and processing was unattainable." I'm sorry, sir, were you able to understand the gist of the paragraph from "Intelligence in the War in Bosnia, 1992 to 1995"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did understand it, Madam. And that is why the gentleman should admire us for the work that we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree. I think under the circumstances you did a fabulous job, but you could not, as you stated in the Krstic trial, know that every intercept was accurate, that every transcription was accurate, that every encryption was accurate. You could not know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to that. I believe counsel has referred to the Krstic trial. She hasn't referred to a particular portion in the transcript. We don't know what the context of that is. We don't really even know what the witness said at that point. So I don't think that was a proper question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe Ms. Sinatra could provide more information on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can, if given one moment and my glasses. Actually, Your Honour, I will come back to this after the break. I know that I can find it, but I'll come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that you know what your testimony was in Krstic, which I will refer to specifically, but you did say that everything was recorded accurately, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go back to the process and the circumstances you were working under, I understand. But the intercepters did miss a lot of the messages, because your intercepter not only had to listen, he had to leave 25 per cent of his time to transcribe and write his notes into a notebook, so he missed a lot of conversations while he was making his rough notes, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For that man, yes, you said that correctly. But I said several times in transcripts from yesterday and other days that some materials were taken at the same time. So you failed to state that we had two devices which were able to do this, they were able to cover the same relay station at the same time. The RRU-801 and RRU-802. So when the RRU-800 was not working, the other one would be working to cover the materials. So this would prevent anything from just being missed. Of course, everything is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you're not saying that you didn't miss conversations. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible for something to get past us, Ms. Sinatra, but as far as we knew, nothing did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And another thing that had to occur was that you had the thankless job of handling this material for the third time and typing it out, didn't you, I'm talking about recording it, transcribing it, and then you were the one responsible for typing it out, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But I didn't do everything. That means that this was done by people for a total of three times. That's what you're trying to say. But, Your Honours, I would just like to go back to the transcription of my statement. It was stated RRU-801 and 802. I apologise. What I said that one position of the equipment was RRU-800 and the other position was also an RRU-800. So I apologise for this correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much for clarifying that for us because you're watching the record a lot easier than I am. But when you say units, are you talking about the RR-800 being at Okresanica and the RR -- the other one that you mentioned being at the other location at Konjuh? They weren't both located at Okresanica, were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I will be very specific. I think that it's really necessary. If you can imagine a table of 4 metres long where these devices for radio monitoring are placed. The first monitor would contain a first set, so a device for receiving the waves. The second one to deal with the frequencies. Then there would be another device to mediate between the second and the third device. And then there was an adaptation system for the UHER in order to receive all the messages as flawlessly or as perfectly as possible in order to avoid any background noise, humming, or anything. The second position would also hold an RRU-800. The third metre would hold such a device. And the fourth metre was hold an RRU as well. So all of this was at Okresanica and it was under my supervision. I hope that I was clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had two units going at one time, each one with the UHER connected to the end; right? When I say "units," I'm talking about electronic equipment. Two series of your electronic equipment running at one time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each one would have its own UHER.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And Your Honours, just for clarity purposes, I have a blank sheet of paper here. I would like it if we could give the witness this blank sheet of paper and let him draw two diagrams. One is a diagram of the flow of the equipment and the second will be a diagram of the building itself, the location of his unit, the location of the 21st unit, the location of the secret service and where they are in relation to each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I just wonder, Your Honour, what the relevance is of all this. Why is it necessary to embark on this exercise at this point? I mean, I don't think it's particularly relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, I wonder if you have a specific case there. I mean, whether those matters will be directly related to your case, your Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Since we are challenging the reliability of the process and if you'll be tolerant -- I'll go ahead and ask him another question, too, just to make this clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the cross-examination of the Blagojevic counsel yesterday, you had stated in the record that you didn't have any way of telling whether the document was generated by you or whether it was generated by the secret service. I believe that the secret service documents were typed in all capital letters and the documents generated by your department were typed in lower case letters. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. What's the problem? I don't understand?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've got to have the relationship of exactly where the secret service office was compared to his unit and how they were all really basically lumped together. I think it's important for the clarity of our examinations, both the Prosecution and the Defence. If you like, I could ask the usher to give him a blank sheet of paper at the break and maybe he could go into that issue and make those drawings at the break for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we may do that during the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'll move forward and come back to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I just want to clarify, Your Honour, one point. Ms. Sinatra made a statement and then she went on and asked a specific question. And I don't necessarily think the statement -- that the evidence was that he had no way of knowing that the document was generated by him or by the state police. She said secret service. I think she was referring to the state police. I just want to -- I just want to make it clear for the record that I don't think that's quite the way the evidence came out yesterday. But she went on and asked him another question and that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Issa, I think if there's anything that you are not clear on, you may revisit it during your re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was no direct telephone line between Okresanica and Tuzla, was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a direct line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Okresanica to Tuzla in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1995 it went via Srebrenik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1995 you stored all of the intercept information on floppy disks and couriered it to the 2nd Corps, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. We did not store them all and send them over, but as the material was filled in, then we would pass those materials on immediately in shifts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In shifts meaning every ten-day period that you changed out your unit. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you never received those floppy disks back, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't need them, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you aren't stating that these were preserved in any way? They were probably not stored, were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, I passed them on for storage and then they became the care of other people. So even if I wanted to respond to that question, I'm not able to. But there are those who could give you a response.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Based on the interviews with a lot of intercept operators from the BiH army, in this book the author says that one of the mottos of the intercept operators was: "In God we trust, all others we monitor." Wouldn't you think that was true of the intelligence service or the communications service for electronic warfare?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm not sure how that's relevant, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I admit. I think it was just interesting. I'll pass it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know with your experience that intelligence is the gathering of secret information, especially for military use, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than secret information, it also means the gathering of other types of information, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it all fit -- secret information is a subtitle of intelligence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but also based on other information, certain knowledge about the enemy can be compiled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And anti-electronic warfare is a part of intelligence of any army, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to go to what has been marked as Defence Exhibit 36.1/3. And again, I apologise that we don't have a translation. But I'm going to page 224. And I just want to ask you if these are -- if you agree that these are disadvantages of intelligence information. Do you agree: Intercepts are always a matter of greatest secrecy, only a need-to-know basis. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And besides the extreme secrecy and limited distribution, there's an inhibition regarding its use. I mean, it could result in life-threatening situations for others, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, let me ask you, isn't intelligence, it was also not valued properly and sometimes not even believed by the people that received the information. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this happens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in many countries, the intelligence and military become too dependant upon intelligence, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure how he can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: If he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that question is too broad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: These are general disadvantages of intelligence. I believe since he is an expert in the anti-electronic warfare unit that may be -- I'm -- not an expert in the term of the Court, but because of his information I would like to just ask him whether he agrees or disagrees with the conclusions on intelligence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- but could you please ask a specific question concerning the work he is engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A lot of time because of the intelligence information provided, the other sources might be dismissed or not looked at carefully. I'm talking about the other sources other than intercepts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, you took only one excerpt and read it out and said that it does not refer to intercepted messages. So could you please tell me, which part are you specifically thinking of? Which part of the intelligence information are you referring to specifically, and which ones do you mean are then dismissed. So could you please tell me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happens when you're listening to electronic warfare communications? You're only getting part of the puzzle. You're not getting the entire picture, are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a lot of times due to situations beyond your control, a lot of times the information arrives too late to be useful to the parties at the time. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that then we are the ones to blame for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not trying to blame anybody. These are just general disadvantages of electronic warfare. But you do agree with me that a lot of times the information arrives too late to assist in the military situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If tactical information is in question, then of course that can arrive too late. But if they are of a command nature, then they have a longer lease on life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, as you stated, even your floppy disks that were sent down to command were on a ten-day shift. So if they didn't receive them until ten days later, in some situations that could be too late, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, this time we didn't really understand each other. You asked me whether there was a direct line of communication with Tuzla, and I said that there was. So we had a computer and a modem through which we sent this on to the command. So each daily report contained this material. This material was sent off and received with this report. But when we're talking about tapes, then it did wait for the shift. If necessary, if the material was very important or significant, then the commander, and I'm just giving you an example, could order somebody to come and pick up this tape, and then this would be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you're really confirming that the tapes, as a rule, were only sent down on a ten-day shift, unless you decided that it was urgent. And under special extraordinary circumstances you could have a tape picked up. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, this is what it looks like: We did not conclude that the material was so important or significant, but the gentleman from the command based on the report would make this conclusion, and then they would send somebody. I apologise, but this is how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And this is a more important disadvantage of electronic warfare. The flow of information is so enormous, but the analysis capability is not sufficient. Analysts must decide is a message is valuable and they're flooded with masses of intercepts, as this author says, unable to see the wood for the trees.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes. I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: It's a little more than that, Your Honour. Frankly, I don't see how this witness could possibly answer that question. I think it's overbroad. It's an opinion from an author. And he's already testified that it wasn't his job to analyse the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I will go into the analysis process in a moment. But I was just trying to get through the basic generic disadvantages of electronic warfare. If he can answer the question, I will simplify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you did not pose a question to this witness. It is just a statement there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. If the Court will allow me to pose a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you may try.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, that there is an enormous flow of information and that the information comes in but there's not enough people there to analyse it, whether it's important, urgent, valuable. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually we would know which channel on a multichannel repeater station were covering civilian stations and which ones were strictly military. So based on that, you could narrow down the number of channels. This question, really, it's a relative thing to evaluate material. You could see which material is interesting in some way. But the material which is not interesting, and you consider it to be interesting, then you could consider that material to be as material that was missed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me just say, it would be a true statement if one of your intercept operators said that what they considered important was dependant on whether the person speaking was important or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be one of the methods, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And another problem with electronic warfare is that signals can be rendered secured and codes can be changed suddenly. Transmitters can frequency hop, false information can be disseminated, and superior cryptology methods could be used by the opposing party. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the limited distribution of intercepted conversations was many times used for personal political ends, wasn't it, not just military decisions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I really don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll skip that one. The next one, though, as a disadvantage of anti-electronic warfare is, many times there was a lack of coordination between the intelligence gathering activity, such as you've pointed out the security service, the military, the headquarters in Tuzla, the headquarters in Sarajevo. One person could gather information and not inform the other intelligence gathering organisation. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, this was a problem pertaining to a higher level. Whether the various sources of intelligence would communicate among themselves and harmonise their activities, well, that was up to them. I delivered my materials regularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. One more general question. The electronic warfare and interception units were also subject to atmospheric disturbances, static, poor reception, occasional dropouts of signals, and it's specifically a disadvantage when intercepting conversations if there are mountains and valleys, right, or even tall buildings in cities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. And that's why the same channel on the same relay station could have dropouts of signals, fadings, because of fog or other conditions, static also. You've listed all the elements, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this might be a good time to take a break. I'm going to be starting another topic. If it's time, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, would you please tell me how long you will last for your direct -- cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have at least one more full session, maybe more than that. This is an important witness for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I hope you could finish your cross-examination during the next sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I hope so, too. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So we'll resume at 10 minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I think this is my last reference to the book, but I was informed you pronounce the name Cees, Cees Wiebes. And I'd like to refer to Defence Exhibit 36.2/3 page 300. And again, I apologise for no translation, but it's a very short statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would just like to ask if the conclusion drawn by the Dutch institute that studied the Bosnian intelligence, that you agree or disagree with it. Page 300: "Taking the Bosnian efforts as a whole, it must be concluded that the service responsible for signals," that's -- you know what signals is, "was simply too undermanned and too poorly equipped to fulfill its mission adequately. Though there were many intercepts, the processing, analysis, and reporting were totally inadequate. Intercepts were not typed out immediately in a word processing programme, but transcribed by hand in a logbook. Tapes bearing messages were reused, and hardly any use was made of computers to process and disseminate the data flow."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I have to tell you that in view of the fact that you have read out a paragraph by, as you say, an eminent expert, writer, or whatever, who wrote about what was happening at the time, about a whole army, what I can say is that I partially agree with what you have read. But for me to know precisely what the conclusion of the book is, I would have to read the whole book, if you will allow me to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that's a very fair answer, and if I had it in B/C/S, I would offer it to you. Trust me. I'm going to go to another subject. Let's go to the content. At Okresanica, you didn't have any people who were considered analysts, people that could analyse the message and assess their value, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, your commander of the 2nd Corps General Said Delic, he did not inform you all or brief you daily of the political and military situations going on, did he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 14th of July, 1995, the 28th Division from Srebrenica - I think they were led by Naser Oric - made a mass exodus from Srebrenica to Tuzla. There were 10.000 soldiers, men, women, and children trying to save their lives, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this is correct, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you received an order from your command telling you to monitor the location and the progress of the 28th Division, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're partly right there, too. It was our task to catch a communication if possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these soldiers coming from Srebrenica, they had hand-held Motorolas with limited battery life, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the same thing you did. As it was our task to try to find out how far they had come to intercept a message or catch a message, and this same applied to a radio relay station as well as to hand-held Motorolas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know that as the 28th Division or the column, as it was called, of Bosnian Muslims was approaching the Zvornik Brigade zone of responsibility, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that later on, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time your order didn't encompass zoning in on the Zvornik area in order to protect and listen and intercept the messages from the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I said everything I know about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you intercepted any messages from the Zvornik Brigade via the relay station, it was only because you were really concentrating on the approach of the column, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was because we were concentrating on one of the relay stations or several relay stations. I know that there was one that would provide more information. There were others we expected information from, but I can't say right now how much information there was. But it was -- what we were focusing on was to get all the information we could. And that's what our orders were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When -- on the July 14th and 15th, during the fleeing of the Bosnian column from Srebrenica, there was heavy combat activity going on in and around Zvornik, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't judge that in any detail at the time, how and where heavy fighting was going on, but we did have some information about this, and this was information coming from the relay equipment, where we found out what you have just mentioned, that they were moving in columns of about 100 men, that at one point they had broken through their lines. That's what I remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, due to this urgent situation of the combat in the area, the fleeing of 10.000 people for their lives, the possible falling of the Municipality of Zvornik, there was unusually heavy radio traffic, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go on to your testimony on Thursday where you testified about the procedure for intercepting a VRS conversation. And I am one of these people that's a bottom-line person. From your testimony I extracted what I believe you described as your procedures. So will you verify, confirm, or deny that these were the procedures of Okresanica July 14th, 15th, 1995. And I'm going to give you a list.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first thing you do is you get some kind of order from your command to look for a special feature, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Madam. In principle, yes. However, if we happen to be on a frequency where there was a conversation going on, whether it was an old frequency or a new one we had come across accidentally by scanning, we could tape that conversation also, even without an order. But in principle, yes, our activities were contingent upon an order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So after you get the order, the next thing you do is you have to redirect your antennas to whatever that order encompasses. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then after you redirect the antennas, you put your earphones on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Madam, where you got these earphones. After redirecting the antennas, we had to find the suitable frequencies, find out if there was any activity there. On more complex relays, we had to find out whether they had pilots, whether there was any interference and what the other characteristics of the relay equipment was. What the route was, what the strength of the signal was. So first they had to be found, recognised, and then monitored. And also the order we received might contain a frequency, that was one of the procedures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I hadn't even put that in my list of things, but ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to add to this that after this entire procedure, what would usually follow in the order would be that we would also look for other frequencies with the same participants, whether another relay route or small relay stations belonging to particular units and so on that would have the same participants. Only when we had done all this would we put on all our earphones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So order, redirect antennas, and then you have to find the frequencies that you're looking for pursuant to the order. Right? Or the relay stations that are stipulated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you put your earphones on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you scan for participants on these frequencies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you record the frequencies if you find one that you're locking into?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're saying now, the scanning meaning looking for participants. But usually we had the frequencies that the same participants had used previously. And also, we would get basic instructions from the command containing the frequencies, and this would be immediately put into operation and we would do the scanning on another set of equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During a combat operation like this, the frequencies change often, don't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then once you decide that you hear a frequency and you hear a conversation and you hear participants, then you have to determine who the participants are -- no, first of all you have to determine whether the conversation is important. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, we could easily be mistaken. We could press the pause button or we could start recording the conversation, because we couldn't tell right away whether it was important or not, and if it wasn't, we could stop the recording.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. You listened for a little bit to determine whether it was important, then you made a decision whether you wanted to record it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, that's what you say. I have said what I have to say in that respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm here to have you tell me, not for me to tell you. But once you determine that it's a conversation you want to listen to, then you have to determine who you think the participants are in the conversation. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then once you determine who the participants are, then you either move to another frequency or you start the tape, whether it's important or not. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, what you are saying runs counter to what I said. I said that on many occasions we could be mistaken as to the first assessment about whether the conversation was important or not. So we would begin recording right away. This happened very often, especially when orders arrived before we got into the activity, we would start recording, and then if it wasn't something for us, we would go back. And at the same time, we would be looking for other frequencies for duplex and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. I thought you did mention the pause button, so sometimes you would start the tape to record and then you would push the pause button until you saw whether it was something you found of interest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did mention the pause button. I said that between conversations it was always on pause. So when we had to start recording, we would press the pause button to start it. But there was another way. The juro button, we would just pull it out. If there was no activity for a long time and then we would depress the button and it would start recording right away, as soon as the conversation started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think what you're saying is once you determined that the conversation was important, you would take the pause button off so it would start recording. Once you got the conversation recorded -- and by the way, did you record the entire conversation when you decided it was important or just a portion of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, it would always be an entire conversation. We weren't always able to intercept the beginning, so the beginning might be missing in some cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then after you recorded the conversation -- or simultaneously it was transcribed into a notebook in handwritten notes. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or simultaneously if it was an easy conversation when there was not much activity going on, when activities were few and far between, when the participants were speaking slowly, the operators were so well practiced that they could note it down right away, and then they would go over it again to check whether they had missed something. But in principle, the procedure was to record the conversation to go back to zero, then to transcribe the conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think what you were just saying is that sometimes they skip the process of hand transcribing into the notebooks. If there was no activity or little activity, they would take right from the tape into the computer. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So it's transcribed handwritten into a notebook, and then once it's put in a notebook is it typed up on the computer first or is it sent to encryption? It's typed up on the computer first, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part of what you said. The first part of what you said, Madam. First it would be typed into the computer. So after recording, transcribing, and copying from the notebook into the computer, it would then be encrypted and sent on to the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's typed into the computer, and encryption gets your -- printed out, computer-typed transcription of the recording. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then these tapes and these notebooks and these floppies were then couriered or after a ten-day shift were sent to the 21st Division, and if they were important enough they would be sent on to the 2nd Corps, or did they go directly to the 2nd Corps? I'm sorry, I know the answer to that. They went directly to the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not how it was, Madam. I apologise. It couldn't go to the 21st Division when I was not a member of that division. I think the procedure has been explained several times. It went to the command of my corps, of my unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about shift changes every ten days. Every ten days you had a new group of people come up, new set of notebooks, new set of tapes, new set of equipment, and you had a debriefing process that you had to go to. So the shift change took a lot of time, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I want to go back to your process. I think you testified before that if you heard a conversation clearly, then you would transcribe it immediately into your written notebook. If you could not hear the conversation clearly, it was written on a little piece of paper to be transcribed later. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I have to draw your attention to the fact that I have already explained this to your colleague, but I will go over it again. When conversations were clear and when they were not clear, and with regard to the pieces of paper, when there was several conversations, they would be taken down on a piece of paper with the basic information, such as the frequency, time, participants, and the counter position. When there was several conversations going on. If there was only one conversation going on, this was not written down on a piece of paper, but it would be put into the notebook. The tape would be rewound and the conversation would be transcribed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying that whether you wrote it in the notebook or whether you wrote it on a little piece of paper had nothing to do with the clarity of the recording whether you could hear it clearly or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You keep saying that if conversations were not clear we transcribed them on a piece of paper. But I have explained what it was that we put on a piece of paper. The conversation itself, regardless of how unclear it was, was transcribed in the notebook word for word. If there was something that was not clear, it would be played back over and over again. And you could call a colleague to help you. That's how it was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So the little pieces of paper were just your rough notes on conversation that you couldn't hear clearly so you could go back and listen to it again. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, she's now asked the witness the same question a number of times and, respectfully I say, has misstated it a number of times. The witness has repeated himself several times. I think his evidence is clear and that's not what he said. And I think, you know, it may be time to now move off this point given that we've now gone over it over and over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we've spent enough time on that subject, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: May I just have him answer the question whether the pieces of paper had rough notes on them so they could go back and review this testimony -- I mean, this recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you like. But we have to move on. You have to remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The little pieces of paper were just your rough notes so you knew to go back and listen to this interception again. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the little pieces of paper were destroyed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the tapes that were sent to the 2nd Corps, were erased or destroyed. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how you came to that conclusion, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we don't have any preservation of the tape recordings that you had at Okresanica in July 1995, do we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, that is your problem or somebody else's problem. I want to be clear about these tapes. I've stated several times, and I will repeat it again, that we sent out completely recorded tapes with all the live material, everything that happened. When there was a lot of material when no more could fit in, then we would pack that -- those tapes and send them on to the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But you've never been played a tape reflecting your notations that you transcribed in July of 1995, have you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say you take notes and you go back and you listen to a conversation to make sure it's transcribed accurately, if there's a poor recording of a conversation, playing it 11 to 15 times over and over again is not going to make it clearer, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes there were parts of conversations that were not complete, but what we were able to determine, what we were able to put down on paper, we did put down on paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so on Thursday you testified that you would rerun it like a disk jockey to identify with 100 per cent certainty. The truth is, you can't identify a poor recording with 100 per cent certainty, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only did I say that on Thursday, I said that a little while ago also. I would return or play back the tapes several times not only myself, all the others would do that, too. There were conversations which we were not able to transcribe 100 per cent. In that, you are right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I just want to add, you even would invite in members of the secret service for an extra set of ears to help determine the accuracy of the recording, but playing over and over again with however many ears you bring in a recording that is not recorded clearly will not make it clear, will it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure that the witness said that he would invite members of the secret service for an extra set of ears. I don't believe that was the evidence at all. And I think that at this point counsel is simply repeating another version of her same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra, you have to rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. I will, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that on occasion members of the secret service would come in -- security service, I'm sorry, would come into your room and assist you in listening to a conversation and filling in the gaps that are in the poor recording?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This did not happen in my presence. If it happened in the presence of some other operator, then you would have to ask him that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not saying it didn't happen. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I never invited any of them to help in the transcription because the staff that we had was quite sufficient. And I said several times that we would call perhaps one person, sometimes they would all be there. But this referred to my unit only, to my shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you listened to a tape over and over again to make it make sense, you mean that you filled in the gaps of what you couldn't understand. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not right. We tried to identify some extra word or tried to see what the reason was why we could not make more of the text available. So these were efforts to try to transcribe a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I just want to go back. I don't know if it assists the previous cross-examination by counsel for Blagojevic, but earlier he was questioning you intensely on periods and exclamation marks. And the truth is, those were really important in transcribing conversations, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But these are main components of a conversation, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to go to the meaning that it had for your unit. For example, dot, dot, dot meant that you didn't understand the rest of the statement. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that between the last word and the next words, a part of the conversation was -- we were not able to understand it. It was either inaudible or unclear, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And an exclamation mark represented a special tone or inflection in the voice, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And an asterisk meant that you missed the rest of the total conversation. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I know exactly what this is about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's about the signals and the codes that you had within your transcription unit, which takes a conversation down, puts punctuation marks in it, and then those punctuation marks have special meaning when that written transcription is transcribed into a computer programme.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They mean something, but I'm not sure about the asterisk coming in for mixed -- for missed text. I don't know whether I said that. It doesn't quite sound to me ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Like you said it or was it just common knowledge for your unit? About the asterisk. You knew about the meaning of the asterisk, although you didn't testify about it to this point. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned the asterisk, Madam, not me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to go on to another topic. The training of the people that worked in your unit, most of them were very young conscripts, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, most of them were under 25 years old. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Madam, you're forcing me now to calculate and to go back and see how old they were at the time. It is my opinion that perhaps a half or at the most or a little bit less than half were of that age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these new conscripts, they came to you with no prior training in radio equipment or communications. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, now if we're talking about the period of 1993 or 1995, we're talking about a majority of people who were radio amateurs and who had already some degree of experience from the beginning of the war in these tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if one of your intercept operators said he had no prior experience but he was trained on the job, he wouldn't be telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wouldn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the witness has answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, all of the important conversations were recorded and sent on to operations people at command. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people in your unit were monitoring a minimum of, like, 24 frequencies at one time. Would that be accurate? I mean, each member on shift was monitoring about 24 frequencies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was only in case one person was on the shift and following 24, but he actually monitored two devices. The scanner itself monitored 24.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you do know that some of the VRS interceptions were spoken in Hungarian and Romanian. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The search for frequencies when you took over a shift, that wasn't done automatically. That was done manually, wasn't it, with the dial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, you're not right. There is a scanner for that as well, and it would go from one frequency to another. But if there was something interesting, you could manually go back and forth. At the same time, you could also combine manual and scanner operations, because with a certain pause we could also pick the frequencies manually. We also had devices like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to bring your attention, if I could, with the assistance of the usher to what was marked as P232.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I don't know if the witness has a copy of P232 -- oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know you're familiar with this intercept. And I just wanted to bring your attention, as previously noted by the Prosecution, /A -- 232/A is an English translation of the handwriting sample which is P232/B, which is -- and then /C is an English translation of the computer typed-out version of 232/D and /E, which are the same conversation. Just for verification, there is no audio tape to support any of these writings in 232. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me, Madam, this is something I don't know. This is something you need to find out from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And without an audiotape, there's no way for us to check on the audio accuracy, is there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And without an audio recording, there's no way for us to go back and use any type of expertise in voice identification, is there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Voice identification is not possible, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you stated, these tapes were used over and over again. If you notice the original /B of 232/B --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is not your handwriting, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you say, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you, is it? That's a question. I'm not ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you stated that the reason you remember this is because you made a notation that the only reason you were able to record this conversation was because a switchboard operator had left the line open. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, the remark was made why they were receiving a conversation in this state, because nobody would understand what was actually going on without this remark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's true, because you're supposedly recording an intercepted telephone conversation, but as you note there are letters BB, JJ, XY, BE. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Except that I allegedly taped it, but everything else is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to go into the fact that we don't have a tape. So we have to rely on what you've written down here. But under your direct testimony on Thursday, you were asked by Ms. Issa which telephone operator you were referring to when you said that one of the lines had been left open at the switchboard. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The switchboard operator from the main exchange. Should I say which participant I mean? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm going to ask you. And you stated that it -- bless you. It was the operator from Badem, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Badem was the code name for the Bratunac Brigade, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know that Mr. Jokic was never a part of the Bratunac Brigade, was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, if we read the text, then we can see that the gentleman who was calling is calling Badem. So the gentleman who called, called the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're stating that the Badem switchboard operator left the line open, not the Zvornik Brigade switchboard operator. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on. Now, Ms. Issa did try to direct your attention to a portion of the intercept where it says -- sorry, "I will. I will. Hello. Hello." Right? She asked you to look at that phrase over and over again, I believe, during direct examination.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, she asked you if there was anything in this sentence that you were listening to that you were uncertain about, didn't she?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. I think this probably needs to be done in private session, Your Honour. But I would like to distribute what could be considered a confidential document that is marked D37/3 for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
