utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to go back to what was marked D36.2/3. And I would like to draw the Trial Chamber's and the Prosecution's attention to page 292, because I have no translation for the witness, and I will have to read it. I will provide the witness with a translation. But I just wanted to verify that this is from the book, but it is citing witness CC from the Krstic trial. Did witness CC tell the truth and is this a truthful statement from the Krstic trial? "Crew of the electronic warfare unit of the 21st Division in Okresanica was small, consisting of three interception positions which were manned around the clock in shifts. Each team worked between four and eight hours a day for a whole week and then had a week off. Operators who intercepted the message made crude notes and worked it out later in their logbooks. These notes were passed on to the commander who typed out the messages on a computer. The intercepts were then sent by courier to the command of the 21st Division for further analysis. Important messages were phoned through immediately to the 2nd Corps in Tuzla. There was no direction-finding equipment and frequencies that were identified on the basis of knowledge of the comment operator, that's the information operator." And that's from witness CC in Krstic. Is that accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, you're asking me a lot. This is about the 21st Division. What have I to do with that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just tell me, what was your relationship with the 21st Division?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't any, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So all of this information about the 21st Division in your unit and the security service being located in one building, it was really just your unit and the security service. Right?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, what does that mean? I mean, I don't quite understand what Defence counsel is asking there, and quite frankly, I haven't objected, but you know up to this point, but a lot of this is not particularly relevant. And I think the witness has pointed out that he isn't really in a position to answer questions in relation to other units. The last question doesn't quite make sense to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, I believe the witness has answered the question already.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. Well, he said there wasn't any 21st Division there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. There wasn't any relations between the two units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: My question is that the 21st Division is a military division. The security service is a civilian organisation. So we have the identification of three separate units at this place and he's only telling us about two. I think it has to do with credibility and testing his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think, you know, you could not get much by asking this kind of question as to the credibility of this witness. How could you ask this witness to tell something of other units?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: No. Just identifying their presence. I'm not asking him to tell what their purpose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the witness has already testified in this aspect.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move forward then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The interception by your unit was made more difficult by the increased use of encryption equipment by the VRS, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Madam. Can you wait just a moment, please. Your Honours, I would like to show Ms. Sinatra this document which she asked me to draw during the break. And if it, she will find the precise answer to what she was asking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I thank you very much. The problem is I can't be provided with the document until the next break, so I will come back to this line of questioning and I appreciate your offering that information to me. But it has to be marked by the registrar and then given to me. So please understand the procedures here. I will talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, since we are on this subject, why don't we use that map, whatever, at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't been provided a copy of it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, us either, but you could have a look at this copy right now. So please show this map to Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, it's in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we could ask the witness to say in B/C/S and the interpreters will translate it into English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So would we put it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think there is no problem. Well, I have been advised that although this document is under seal, we could put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Sinatra, please pay attention now to this room I am pointing out right now and what it says here, 21st Division. This gives you the answer to the question you put. I think it's all right now, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what DB is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the service of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that would be the security service -- state security service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: State security, that is a service of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there's another room next to the 21st Division that has two doors going in and out of it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, this double door here is entrance number 2 used by the state security and the 21st Division. And this was a wall separating them and us. And these were the rooms belonging to my unit, this part here. I apologise for the proportions which may not be quite correct, but all the elements you asked of me are here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I appreciate that. It's very illuminating. When you say there's a wall there, so when you shared information with the state security services, you had to go outside and come in another door?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I would like to have an opportunity to analyse this in a moment. I don't know what it says. But I assume from the wall over -- but I know the KZ is the encryption department or KZU. Right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Madam. I do apologise. KZ, that's what it means. I think that this also will be familiar to you. This is the first room to the left from the entrance. This is the monitoring centre where our activities were carried on, the ones we are discussing now. This is the corridor. This is a dormitory, and this is a kitchen and living room. And this is another small corridor. I didn't have an eraser, which is why I crossed out this little line here. So this is another small corridor from which one entered the kitchen and the duty room of the 2nd Corps communications centre. So the person on duty belonging to that unit would be here. Here we have a storage area and the commander's bedroom, that would be my bedroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first door to your right when you enter from your side, you said that's where your communications centre was located, is that where you had the two 4-metre long tables?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam. I have just said that this is the communications centre of the 2nd Corps. That's what it says here, and the person on duty had his room here. And there was a man working here and by mistake I put a bed in the kitchen -- actually, it should be in here, in this little room. So this bed here in the living room was actually in here, but I made a mistake, you know. And the room that you have just mentioned, this is that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Just for clarification purposes, the -- I had talked about that room where it says DB as being a MUP facility, Ministry of the Interior, but that's not actually correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't the state security service, isn't it more -- instead of the FBI, it's more like the CIA or the KGB, it's a more secret operation than the MUP?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know how relevant this is. My submission is it's totally irrelevant and I don't think the witness is in a position to make those kinds of conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, that comparison is not proper.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: If you would just allow me to ask the one next question I will make it relevant and proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may try.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Isn't the state security service a more secret group than the MUP; right? This is a precursor. I haven't come to the other question. I have to get a yes or no on this one first. Okay. I'll go ahead and ask it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, this state security service later became the AID which is the one that is in control and custody of the tapes from 1995?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I hate to ask a compound sentence, but I had to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking me a lot again. Whether this service later became the AID, well, we referred to it as the DB. That's what we called it, DB, and that's what it stayed. And I'm mentioning the name that we used at the time. DB was the department of the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior that was stationed here. And it's common knowledge what they were doing there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since this is -- you've testified before this Tribunal before regarding this same subject. I wanted to ask you if you are aware that in your last testimony there were audiotapes supporting the intercepts that you were discussing, whereas there are not audiotapes in this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm certainly not aware of that and if there's portion of his testimony that Ms. Sinatra wants to point him to, she certainly can do that, but I don't think it's a proper form to ask the question in the manner that she did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- but the -- in the cross-examination the Defence is entitled to ask this question first. And later on, the Defence may show some evidence to rebut any answers given by this witness. Let's hear what the witness is going to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Sinatra, would you repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified in another case, the Krstic case, before this Tribunal and as so, when you testified about your notes on intercepts, you also heard an audiotape that supported those notes, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And although we have several A, B, C, D, and E, D and E of 232 -- P232 are really the same interception just typed by two different units. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there's no corroborating simultaneous recording from, say, Konjuh or another communications location, is there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'd like to bring out also -- earlier today or earlier yesterday, I believe, P231. The witness was questioned on that. If we could look at P231, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're familiar with your previous discussion on P231. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do remember some things. I don't know what you're going to ask me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I want to go to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, eight spaces up from the end of this document, and your notes, are the written notes 231/B. Sir, could you just read that to me, the part that is in italics, "pronovo jaci." Could you read that, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in line 8 from the end. It says: "Well, now my boys are now in the western part. Working there as of today. Everything is in place. Sweet as a nut."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I'm looking for the part that's in parenthesis. I think that it's maybe ten lines up then. It's a part that says -- the line starts with: "I understand completely," then we'll focus on one down there. Then there's a portion in parenthesis, and I'm sorry for my pronunciation, but it starts with "pronovo jaci." Could you read that in your language, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The translation, I find it funny. It says: "Because," and then parenthesis, (in the continuation drowned out again), it says (by previously recorded conversation).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And this was from the document you were discussing earlier. That's all I wanted to illuminate from that document. Thank you. Now, I want to go back to the people that analyse whether -- or monitor whether a conversation is important or not. You testified earlier that -- that you testified in the Krstic trial that the operators were not briefed by the army on the military circumstances. Right?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this. It's one thing to put a question to the witness, for example, were the operators briefed, et cetera. But to put it in the form that she's putting it in, it's improper. If she's going to suggest to him that he testified in a particular manner, that I think she needs to point to the exact portion of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I believe that Ms. Issa is incorrect here. If the witness can remember from his own personal knowledge about his testimony, I don't have to point to a record. If he remembers, he can testify about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, for the record, I totally agree with Ms. Sinatra. It is totally proper, the form of the question. This is classic cross-examination before confrontation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as I said before that this kind of cross-examination is allowed, but at the same time, Ms. Sinatra, I have to remind you of the time. We are almost finished this sitting. I wonder how long are you going to use.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to say that I have at least 30 more minutes, maybe more of cross. I could sit here at the next break and I may have duplicated some questions. Can I cut and consolidate, but I think I still have 30 minutes conservatively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You know, at the beginning of this afternoon's session, we told everybody that we would like to have this witness go back home tomorrow morning. This witness has been in The Hague for quite a long time. Of course, there are three days in between that we were not sitting. Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry to hold him over, Your Honour, but he has important information. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these people that were making the decisions on what conversations were important and what were not were young conscripts, people taught on the job, and people who had not been briefed about the military circumstances surrounding them. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Previously you asked me whether the commander briefed us daily. From time to time we were briefed on the military situation, but not on a daily basis, as you put it in your question. I think I've already answered that question. Yes, you observed rightly that these were young people, but they were experienced ham radio operators, and they were people who started doing this job as soon as the war started. So by this time they would have gained quite a great deal of experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not all of them had previous amateur radio operator experience, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, going back to briefing and whether they were informed, you stated in your testimony on Thursday that the army did not tell you why they asked for certain intercepts, "You were working in the dark." Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I really don't remember working in the dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But they didn't brief you or they didn't tell you why they asked for certain focus on intercepts. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, as you yourself have said, we had debriefings at the shifts and the officer from the command carrying out the change of shift would go through the information and he would brief the men and so on. So this was the regular procedure, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the decisions on whether a conversation was deemed important or not was made by the intercept operator listening to the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If certain activities were found to be on a certain channel and one started monitoring conversations, there was no need to decide whether a conversation was important or not. All such conversations would be recorded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you're saying that the decision to record a conversation was not discretionary with the intercept operator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was easy for him to tell which conversation was civilian and which was military. They were also very familiar with the distribution of channels, so this was not a problem for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question. Are you telling us that the decision on whether to record a conversation was not totally discretionary with the intercept operator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was. It was up to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when a conversation was deemed important and it was transcribed, only part of the conversation was transcribed -- only the part that this operator deemed important, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, are you trying to say that there are conversations like that? Well, I think that there are several such conversations where previously the conversation was purely of a private nature so that the operator -- yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In fact, when only part of what the intercept operator deemed important, that's the only part that was put into the computer. The rest of it was erased or destroyed; it was discarded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, what you have just said seems to deepen even more and more the statement that you gave about the text. I did say that there was such a text, but globally it was not the procedure to work in that way. A conversation regardless of how many moments it contained which were no longer interesting were not something that we made the decision of. It's possible that the conversation would turn around suddenly. So then we would begin recording. So perhaps this is the situation that you seem to be looking for, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask a long question which involves your procedure. And just to get it straight, you catch a frequency of an intercepted conversation midway through the conversation on many occasions. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would happen, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then when you've recorded part of a conversation, sometimes, especially in the middle of combat, only part of that partially recorded conversation would be transcribed. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I don't see any interdependence there. One thing did not depend on the other. Let me respond first to the first part of your question. If it should happen that we came up to a conversation which was already in progress, we would record it and then we would have a recording of that part of it. As far as the second part of the question, that did not have to be so closely related to whether there was combat or not. Major combat operations may not call for major activity on our equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think what I was trying to ask you is: Most of the time you record part of a conversation on the reel-to-reel tape, and then after part of the conversation is recorded, only the part of the conversation that is deemed important would be transcribed in the notebook. And that would be especially true during a time of intense combat operations. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, the part of the conversation that we heard, that part would be recorded. When we came up against a part of a conversation which was already in progress, that is what you said, from the moment we came upon that conversation, we would record that conversation. We would not leave anything out. There would be nothing that needed to be left out. It wasn't up to us to decide. There were people whose duty it was to decide whether something should be left out or not, but that wasn't us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if another intercept operator from your unit stated that not a complete -- only the important parts of a recording many times were transcribed, he would not be telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, that's an improper form of the question. A witness can't be -- it's not relevant that -- a witness can't comment on the voracity of a potential other witness or whatever Ms. Sinatra happens to be referring to, a previous witness. And frankly, Your Honour, we've been over and over this. I'm not really sure how much further we're getting along by re-asking the same questions over and over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra, I think this is not a proper question to ask this witness. It's quite a hypothetical question. And it's time for the break. If you feel proper, we'll break now, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But after the break I think you'll have 15 minutes to finish your cross-examination. And we'll resume at 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We're back. I would like to distribute what has been marked as P34 -- I mean, D34/3 for identification purposes, and I would like to have the witness look at it, please. Yes, sir, I just want you to answer if you can identify these notes. Do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are notes from my notebook, from my diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these are your personal notes that you took an July 14th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what precipitated these notes was the changing of the shift. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for clarity, the shifts in July 1995 were the 4th of July through the 14th of July. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the next shift also began on the 14th through the 24th. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you stated before that during a shift change, that's the time you bring supplies in, you brief the new people coming in, you make all these notes of personal things that are taken care of on the shift change. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to bring your attention to your notes, and if you see the -- there's an underlined part with a check next to it, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, on the eighth line, I believe, and if I've miscounted, you know what line I'm talking about, right. It's the only one that's -- no, it's the second one that's underlined in your notes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a warning, Madam?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm just asking for your cooperation so that I don't have to go sentence by sentence. But it is --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour -- I'm sorry there seems to be a bit of confusion. The witness -- there is a word referring to warning in the transcript, and the witness may have just been trying to figure out where he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't realise what he was talking about. But there is -- on the line down there I would like to read in the English translation what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you can confirm or deny. "The UHER 2," I think that means 2 UHERs, or the UHER labelled 2 or 1, I'm not quite sure, "was taken to be repaired. It's number 045612, type 1424." So this UHER, type 1424, had been experiencing recording difficulties prior to July 14th, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the 14th of July, this UHER was broken, so that's why it was laid aside. When it broke down, at that point, it was substituted with one in reserve or -- I assume by an UHER number 4. This was the UHER that was at a different work location, the RRU-1. So we have the first work station, that's this UHER. So it could have been substituted or the frequencies from UHER 2 were passed on to or transferred on to UHER 4. I apologise, there is even the possibility that we did have a reserve one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But it also notes in your notes that it was returned on the 17th of July, 1995. Right? If you're looking --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I want to bring your attention again to that Prosecution ERN number which ends in 144, which I believe you're looking at. It says: "Amir took the old UHER, the 1423 type. He brought two adapters for the UHER." Right? "And he took an old adapter from an UHER type 1424." Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So before July 17th -- well, that's all I have to question from this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to lay the proper foundation, this -- these notes that you're looking at you recognise as your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were taken from the notebooks which you brought the Prosecution when you came or which you promised to provide when needed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when you returned to The Hague this time you didn't bring these notebooks with you, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you said, Madam. I did bring them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Because the Prosecution made me think that they had to send for them. I hope you did bring them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not true. First of all, the book had been photocopied about a year ago and was disclosed to counsel. She had the entire book. And pursuant to a particular question that Ms. Sinatra asked us, and at the time I personally wasn't aware that the book had been photocopied about a year ago and given to her, I made a point of ensuring that these pages were photocopied so that we could disclose them to counsel because the witness did happen to have his personal diary with him at the time. So she has had these for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, your comments are quite unnecessary, taking into consideration the time limits.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you and I appreciate Ms. Issa using up five minutes of my time -- just teasing. Okay. I want to go now distribute what has been marked for identification purposes as D33/3, if we could secure the assistance of Madam Usher. I feel like I'm in a football game and the time is running out to make that touchdown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I know that you are not -- you have maybe not been provided this document by the Prosecutor, but these are supposedly -- these are intercepted conversations and indexed to them and the intercepted conversations provided by the Office of the Prosecutor that had been seized from the BiH headquarters in Mostar. They were seized by SFOR. All I want you to do is thumb through the ones in B/C/S and look at the chronological order of the dates for July 1995. To assist, maybe if you thumb through and open it up in the middle, you'll come to the 13th of July, but take your time and thumb through them, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe these have anything to do with this witness. They are completely irrelevant and I don't see how the witness could possibly answer any questions in relation to these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I didn't see any relevance either, Ms. Sinatra. Could you shed some light on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just want to note that these were respected by the Prosecutor as intercepts that had to do with July 1995. Our witness is in charge of the anti-electronic warfare division of an area of the BiH army. What is significant is that I would like for him to look through here. There are intercepted conversations on every day except for the 14th of July. If he can just tell us that he's looked through these intercepts, he knows what they're about, and he recognises that there are no intercepts on the 14th of July. It jumps from the 13th to the 15th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, do we have the English translation for the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour I don't have an English translation. I have an index in English provided by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm objecting to any questions to be put to this witness. There's no foundation that he knows anything about this. Whatever inference that Ms. Sinatra is trying to draw from these documents has absolutely no foundation. I mean, giving a bunch of documents to a witness and saying do you see anything there that refers to the 14th of July is just improper and it doesn't assist in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we haven't heard the question put by the Defence. Let's hear the questions first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do these look like intercepts that were traditionally under the procedure of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way in which I was ordered to hand over documents, this document does not seem to be to me done in that particular way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying you don't believe they area authentic intercepted conversations for July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, to keep interjecting at this point. But that's a clear misstatement of the evidence. That's not what the witness says. He's clearly indicating he doesn't recognise them, which is what I was trying to say before. They're not relevant to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'll just ask him one more question and I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification. The witness never said he doesn't recognise them. He doesn't recognise the form. I think there needs to be maybe another question or to two. But I don't think the witness has indicated that he doesn't recognise anything in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may ask some questions along this line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with the communications centre that recorded these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll save it for another witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Just, Your Honour, for purposes of clarification, again I apologise for having to jump up, but I'm actually informed that these intercepts that Ms. Sinatra has referred to were actually taken by the Croatian army. I just want Your Honour to be aware of that so there's no confusion, perhaps. And that may just settle the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much for that clarification. But Ms. Sinatra has already told us that she will save that document for other witnesses. So I believe that this document will not be the subject of the matter of this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask a follow-up question on your procedure. You know, you said that you were undermanned and understaffed. Under -- you weren't provided with enough tapes and you didn't have enough equipment and you didn't have replacement parts for the equipment. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, may I add to what you have just said. Also that everything that we had at our disposal had to be utilised and I had to make sure that the job was done as well as possible. That's the only thing that I can say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I certainly appreciate your position that you were in in 1995. But undermanned and understaffed, as we've talked about before, you recorded these tapes and then you transcribed them in a notebook, when did you have time to go back and listen to the tapes 11 to 15 times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, you are using the data 11 to 15 times very nicely. It was just about one word or one sentence that this pertained to, so this had to do with just one conversation that was critical, that was difficult to transcribe. So please, do not use this piece of information as if it applied to all the other intercepted conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's just take it in general. When did you have time to re-listen to tapes over and over again? You didn't, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to go into private session for the last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I mean, I have further questions, but I know my time has run out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. Any re-direct, Ms. Issa?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour. Re-examined by Ms. Issa:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, one of the last questions that you were asked in relation to having the time to listen to the tapes over and over again, can you clarify what you meant by that, given your previous evidence that you listened to the tapes over and over again to make sure that you understood a particular word or sentence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Your question is not in line with the question Ms. Sinatra put as to whether we played a tape 11 or 10 or 15 times and how we could find the time to listen to all this. I was quite specific in my response. So what I was talking about was listening to the text and the procedure. Until the material is transcribed and entered into the computer, it is listened to as many times as is necessary for it to be clear and for it to be handed in. After that, there was no longer any reason for us in the unit to listen to that material. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I don't have anything further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: If I might, I have one further follow-up question based on Ms. Issa's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, there's no kind of procedure on that. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us, what was the most important objective in your unit's work.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective in my unit's work was to gather as much information as possible about the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Would you say that there were occasions that the exactness had to give way for quickly passing on information to your command and superiors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, but that was not for me to judge. Only circumstances could indicate something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And my last question: During Ms. Sinatra's cross-examination, you agreed that the JNA and the VRS shared information. Could you please clarify what time period this refers to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is a very good question. This refers primarily to the beginning of the war, perhaps the first year of the war, 1992, and possibly part of 1993 when I was in the 1st Brigade unit doing the same work. There we had information as to how the colonel was attending meetings and giving briefings and asking for the current situation in connection with certain attacks. And in this way, we would get very significant information, because as a colonel deployed in the VRS in a narrow area in the town where I lived and carried out this work, at the meeting of the Main Staff in Belgrade, he would attend. And you can find information about this in the material. I think the material must exist because I handed it into my command. Another example was in large-scale operations and attacks on a narrow part of our defences, the officers of the VRS would establish telephone contacts with other higher-ranking officers, and they would state the location of the columns where they were going, what they were taking with them, and they would specify the material that was to be delivered. I am speaking from memory, so you will excuse me if I get my numbers a little wrong. But for example, they would be discussing several trailer trucks of looted goods, also ammunition, heavy weapons, such as howitzers, large calibre guns, multiple rocket launchers, and so on, as well as ammunition for tanks and they would even have the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-117 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge's questions? Ms. Issa?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, are there any documents to tender? Ms. Issa?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'd -- sorry, at this stage I'll be tendering P318, 321, 346, which I would be seeking to tender under seal, that's the list of members of the witness's unit; P349, which refers to the witness's name, which I would also be seeking to tender that under seal as well; and P312, which is the index to the code names. Now as for the remaining exhibits, P231, 232, 322 and 323, I would be moving to tender those documents. Those are the notebooks and the intercepts. At the end of the calling of the intercept witnesses, I would be moving to tender all of the intercepts at that point, Your Honours. Those are the intercepts that are largely contained in the binders, as well as, I believe, the additional pages that reflect 231/E and 232/E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much for your cooperation and I hope when you are tendering those documents of intercepts, please provide us with a list listing all those intercepts that you are going to tender. I mean at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I might just want to clarify that there is an index that we've provided at the beginning of the first binder that contains the lists of all the intercepts that we intend to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any objections to those documents tendered by the Prosecution? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Not to the ones that were tendered. But one comment with respect to the intercepts. I would suspect that only intercepts that are being discussed in this courtroom through witnesses will be tendered. Any other intercepts we will be objecting to, specifically given the Prosecution's objection to having witnesses discuss intercepts other than the ones that the intercept operators are commenting on in court. So that's why I believe that if they do intend -- and I'm just doing this out of a courtesy so everyone knows where I stand. If they do intend to introduce intercepts, we will object to any intercepts being introduced that have not been brought into court and questioned or foundation laid by the particular individual that actually wrote the intercept at the time and listened to the transcription. But as far as the material being proffered at this time or tendered, we have no objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, any comments, Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It would be my submission at the end of the day that we would have provided the foundation for the tendering of all of the intercepts, given the evidence that Your Honour has heard today and that Your Honours will be hearing for the remainder of this week. As for Mr. Karnavas's comment regarding my objection to that particular intercept, as I believe I indicated before, Mr. Karnavas was trying to put a question to the witness that came from a different platoon. And that was the reason I was objecting, not because -- I wasn't objecting to an intercept that came from the platoon that the witness is part of. And that's the distinction. And I think that's a viable one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honour. The individual that had just testified did lay what I would call a tentative or a partial foundation. Clearly the witness is not qualified to go through every single one of those handwritten intercepts that are in the notebooks. He's only qualified to testify about the ones that he actually listened to and wrote down. And the ones that he was shown here were indeed, as I believe, his and that's why he was able to reflect and comment upon them. So unless the -- this particular witness is willing to say that he can comment on each and every one of them, and that hasn't been laid, that foundation hasn't been laid, the questions haven't been posed, I don't believe that the entire notebook comes in. So if the Prosecutor wishes for the Court to review at the end of the trial certain intercepts, they need to bring in the intercept operators that will lay the proper foundation for every single intercept, not merely as they're doing with this particular witness as if he's a summary witness in saying that these are the notebooks, and I vouch for everything that's in there. So I think that would be improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, do you have any objections to those documents tendered by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do. Although I believe that Mr. Karnavas is correct in the fact that this looks like instead of a summary witness, it almost appears as -- I don't want to use this term, but intercept dumping. Because they're throwing two notebooks of intercepts with no foundation at us. But besides a improper foundation, Your Honour, we object to the introduction of P -- I think it is. Are these the right numbers, 322 and 323?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: That refers to the two notebooks, Your Honour. I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Any intercepts -- until the proper reliability has been established, until all the evidence has been gathered by this Trial Chamber, which the admissibility is to be determined later, because we're challenging. It's not our burden of proof. It's the proof on the Prosecution to prove they are reliable, not our burden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we are not talking about those intercepts that are not tendered. We are going to talk about the documents tendered by the Prosecution, which she kindly announced the number. Do you have any objections to those documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: We approve and concur with the introduction of all documents that are not intercept related or notebook related. And so I believe we agree, if I'm -- I just want for clarification, we're talking about P 318, P 321, and P 346?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And two more.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I missed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: P 349 that is under seal because of the name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And P 312.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And that was a map, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: We have no objections. Thank you very much for helping me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Those documents tendered by the Prosecution are admitted into the evidence. Are there any documents to tender on the Defence part? Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yesterday there was a request that we have the two documents transcribed -- translated; we've done that. And so I've consulted with Mr. Registrar and the Prosecution. And so what is -- the English version translation of P249/B should have a number of D73/1. And the English translation of P249/D should have an identify -- a Defence identification number of D74/1. And I made references to these through this gentleman, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Can you brief us what these documents are about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Yesterday I cross-examined the gentleman with respect to the Prosecution's evidence that was marked for identification purposes as P249. As you will recall, there was a line of questioning with respect to sharing of information between the army and the state security services. Initially there was a denial. At some point there was a partial admission. Later on there was a total admission. And these two reports, these -- this particular exhibit, which is I believe from A to E, demonstrated that. At one point in time, I tried to have the gentleman read a portion of one of the documents, and I believe, Mr. President, you requested that I get a translation. So in keeping with the request and the procedure, I made that -- I had it done. And so as a result, I'm requesting that P249/B, the translated version of it be entered into -- be tendered as part of our evidence as D73/1 and P249/D be entered -- be tendered as D74/1. And I do believe, Mr. President, that I will be referring to these documents with the next witness. So I can revisit that issue as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are those documents intercepts?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They are -- one is an intercept, Your Honour. The other one is the daily report, is the daily report. If I may -- and I know it's late and we all want to go home, but if you will recall, Mr. President, yesterday I brought to the attention a particular daily report that was dated 16 July, 1995. And below it it demonstrated that actually the daily report contained information which the gentleman's unit had obtained from and was incorporating into the daily report from the state security services. That would be, I believe, the document with the Prosecution number of P249/D. And then I also showed the gentleman 249/B which is actually the document generated by the state security services themselves, demonstrating that they had in essence incorporated this entire line of intercepts starting with number 652. And the one in particular that I was most interested in was 655, which apparently -- which I understand the Prosecution had or will be making references to. And I wanted to -- the date is of some critical importance. So I didn't make references to them. These were intercepts that we received from the Prosecution. Part of it was not translated by the Prosecution. In fact, only the part dealing with intercept number 655 was. So I had the entire document -- these entire two documents translated, lest there be any confusion, misunderstanding, or allegations that somehow we're being less than complete in your work product.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections, Ms. Issa?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I actually haven't seen those translations, frankly. Although I know that Ms. Stewart was informed that they -- that Mr. Karnavas has actually went ahead and translated these documents. I am wondering, however, and Mr. Karnavas has indicated that he was in a position to tender them at a later point through the next witness, I'm just wondering if perhaps it would be more appropriate to wait at that point, given that we didn't have the translations during the questioning of this witness. But I leave that to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is there any possibility to tender those documents through the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well -- thank you, Your Honour. Yes, we can -- we will be using them through the next witness because -- in fact, it might save us a lot of confusion, because the next witness, they are actually hand and glove. So this one and the other one will have total foundation. Just for the record, the translation was done by the Registry. So it is an official translation not our Karnavas translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Since the Prosecution -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry to have to interject right now. I'm not quite clear. Is Mr. Karnavas withdrawing his offer of these documents into evidence? Because we have objections to them. Should we just withhold our objections until the next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may express your objections for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The objections, of course, are - I hate to use this term - you're either pregnant or you're not. You either accept the intercepts as admissible and reliable or you don't. I don't believe we can pick or choose. Our position is that none of the intercepts are admissible into evidence because they are not reliable. On the other hand, Ms. Issa and the Prosecutor, their position is that they're introducing these intercepts to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Jokic had knowledge and was part of this joint criminal enterprise. Mr. Karnavas is using them to impeach the witness. So they have different purposes at this point and I wanted to differentiate that. Any admission based on reliability, based on a proper foundation laid by the Prosecution is objected to by the Jokic Defence team. There is another purpose for impeachment purposes. Like I said, we can't condone it. But I do understand that there are two different purposes we are dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much for drawing our attention to that important point. Well, Mr. Karnavas, since there is objections from the Defence team and the since those are all the intercepts, I believe that we should hold the consideration of whether to admit them into the evidence or not until a later stage. And maybe together with the Prosecution's intercepts, documents at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I understand you correct, Mr. President -- well, with the -- after the next witness I would be tendering it, but as I understand the rules of evidence as they apply to this Tribunal which are quite distinct from what exists in the Anglo-Saxon world. Tendering is a lot different than actually admitting them into evidence and then we go through the process of how much weight, if any, to give to it. So I will be asking the -- I will be tendering the documents after the next witness, and I understand Ms. Sinatra's position, the Jokic's team position. I fully support their position. However, as was aptly pointed out, we have a different case and that is a decision that the Court will have to make at some point whether there is reliability. As far as tendering, as I understand the rules, you can tender anything and then it is a matter for the trial Bench to decide the next series of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in our mind I think concerning of those intercept documents and after we hear all those witnesses, we'll give each party seven days to file their written objections on those intercepts. And then we'll consider whether we will admit them into the evidence or not. This rule applies equally to the Prosecution as well as to the Defence team concerning the intercepts. So at this stage we are not going to admit these two documents into the evidence. We will leave it until a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe in two weeks. Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I just wanted clarification. You said seven days after all of the intercept witnesses. Are you talking about just the Prosecution's intercept witnesses and not after the Defence has put on their intercept witnesses, seven days after that point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it depends whether there's any objections from the Prosecution concerning your intercept witnesses in the future. If in the future there is an objection from the Prosecution, I think this rule is also applied to your witnesses in your case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm just trying to clarify, after the last witness that is scheduled for this week, then we have seven days to respond and write our written objections?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have to be very cautious on those evidence and we want to give the parties a full opportunity to express their views concerning these documents. Since those documents were regarded as very important in this case. Thank you. Ms. Sinatra, do you have any documents to tender into the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have several documents to tender. I believe there's D32/3 which is the pictures of the equipment used by this witness, if he identified it. There's D34/3, which are the witness's personal notes from his notebooks that he took regarding -- I think it's regarding the maintenance of the equipment. And D36.1/3 which is an excerpt from the book "Intelligence and the War in Bosnia, 1992 through 1995," Cees Wiebes. And D36.2/3 is a same excerpt from the same -- I mean, not the same excerpt but a different excerpt from the same book. Then there is D37/3 which for purposes of this court I believe needs to be filed under seal. And that's it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How about D38/3? That is the map drawn by this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Oh, yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry. It was the diagram. Yes, we do offer the diagram of the information centre, D38/3, personally diagramed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections? Ms. Issa.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I am objecting to the following: I'm actually objecting to 32/3, because as I understand it the witness has indicated that the photographs didn't quite match what he was using at the time. 34/3, the witness's personal notes, I believe the witness was asked specific questions in relation to those notes. He already testified from those notes. To now submit the notes would be taken potentially out of context. And given that he's already given testimony on it, it's not necessary at this point to submit the notes. D36.1/3 and D36.2/3, those are the excerpts from the book that Ms. Sinatra referred to. Again, she only pointed out particular portions of that book. The witness disagreed with much of those portions. Again, in my submission it's not appropriate to simply take out excerpts of a book and submit them into evidence. They're completely out of context. We already have live testimony with respect to the portions that she quoted, statements that she quoted in any event. I'm also objecting to the information report going in for the same reason, 37/3, given that the witness has explained his -- in his testimony in relation to that particular sentence, the "I will, I will. Hello. Hello," from the intercept. And for all those reasons, those are the documents I'd be objecting to. I'm not objecting to the remainder which I believe is the sketch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As far as D32/3, I believe that the witness did identify this RUP-12 as the equipment that he was familiar with and he had used before. And he did say that he used the -- he owned one of these walkie-talkies -- it's not a walkie-talkie, but the second picture, the FT23R, he said he personally owned one of those. And I believe, he testified today about the antenna. He referred to it himself during his testimony, so I believe that that's totally admissible. The witness did testify about it. His personal notes in his diary on the maintenance of the equipment is seminal in this case. It's most important. Although he testified to it, the document itself impeaches the reliability of the equipment we're that talking about and which is the centre of the objections in our case -- not the centre, but one of the many centres. And I believe his notes, which he identified as his own handwriting, he discussed, they are appropriate to be filed as a record in this case. And I think it totally admissible. As far as the excerpts from the book go, we'll withdraw those introductions of those excerpts. He did testify to it. Although he did agree on many times, especially the 12 disadvantages of the intelligence information. He agreed, I would say, 90 per cent of the time. The D37/3 which is filed under seal, the document itself impeaches what the witness said, not what he comments on the document. So the document is used to impeach the credibility of this witness. It's admissible. I provided it to the Trial Chamber under seal because it was a work product of the Prosecution and it's most important that it remain part of the record as -- because he didn't comment on it. I introduced it. He recognised it. And then I moved forward, because I didn't think it was appropriate for him to comment on -- he recognised the people in it, he understood what it said. I think it's totally admissible. And I don't think she's objected to the drawing by this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I think the document D38/8 there's no objections from the Prosecution. It is admitted into the evidence. As for the document D32/3, as Ms. Sinatra said, the witness gave the testimony about those equipment, so we believe they should be admitted into the evidence. As for D34/3, these are the witness's personal notes dated July 1995. As the Defence said that some of the documents will be used to impeach the credibility of the witnesses, we believe this document is this kind of evidence, so it's admitted. As for D36.1 and .2, I understand that the Defence team has already withdrawn, generally speaking, those books which are publicly available are not admitted into the evidence unless they are closely related to the subject matter of this case. As for D37/3, this is an information report. According to our Euro practice, these kind of documents are not admitted into the evidence. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to D34/3, given that you've admitted it, I would ask that it be admitted under seal to protect the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is admitted under seal. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. I'm sorry to have kept you so long in The Hague. And we all wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would only like to make a comment about the procedure of Mr. Karnavas's cross-examination. A document was offered to me for recognition, which was a copy of a document, and that's not how I originally recognised any of the documents. All the documents I recognised were originals. And to help Mr. Karnavas, this may not be so important anymore, but for the gentleman to know, I want to say that I know it's not my document 100 per cent, but I was afraid that copies of documents might contain pages from my unit. Thank you all, ladies and gentlemen, and I wish you good luck in your future work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may leave now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As for the map drawn by the witness, I hope that the Defence team or the registrar could have it translated into English, to have the English subtitles. Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We can have it translated by tomorrow. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just two minor housekeeping matters since we have a few moments left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Oh, good. If we could go into private session just for one of the matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I have to remind the parties that the time at our disposal is limited, so we have to make the best time available in direct or in cross-examining the witness. We have been warned by the Victim and Witnesses section that those witnesses that have been in The Hague for quite a long time and there is unnecessary duration for them, especially for the next witness, he has been here waiting to testify the whole afternoon. But we have to send him back and call him back tomorrow. So I hope that both parties should make the best use of their time. And I also remind the parties the Trial Chamber has the right to cut short the direct examination as well as the cross-examination. Well, it's 7.00, so the hearing is adjourned until tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
